description: InnovaX is a team of SLIIT undergraduates competing to win NASA Space Apps Colombo. We are building real-time astronaut health monitoring software for deep-space missions to track vitals, detect anomalies, and support decision-making. Looking for AI/ML devs, UI/UX designers, data managers, and writers to join us!
summary: EarthScope is a free, web-based "trend detective" tool letting anyone discover what is changing in the Earth system, where, how much, and whether that change is statistically significant. Users pick an Earth science variable (air temperature, relative humidity, or surface soil wetness from NASA’s MERRA-2 model via the NASA POWER API), choose any place on Earth (a point, rectangle, country, or hand-drawn polygon), and select a period from 1981 to the present. EarthScope retrieves the real monthly NASA data, builds and visualizes the time series, calculates the rate of change (OLS regression and Sen’s slope with 95% confidence intervals), and tests significance using the regression t-test and Mann-Kendall test, plus autocorrelation-aware versions (Hamed–Rao and Newey–West) so results are not overconfident. A Spatial Trend Explorer maps every grid cell's trend across a region, revealing how one variable can rise in one area and fall in another, using false-discovery-rate correction across cells. Every result is explained in plain language, including what it does not show. This directly answers the challenge by turning NASA’s vast Earth data catalogue into clear, testable evidence for students and the public with no coding, downloads, or API keys needed. Because climate change is felt locally yet trustworthy local trend analysis remains out of reach for most, EarthScope makes NASA data accessible, rigorous, and transparent, with every number traceable to its exact NASA request.
details:
EarthScope is a web application that turns users into Earth system "data detectives". It answers four questions:

- What is changing? Users choose from Earth science variables produced by NASA’s MERRA-2 model: air temperature at 2 m (T2M), relative humidity (RH2M) and surface soil wetness (GWETTOP). Each variable has a plain-language definition, its unit, data source and coverage notes (for example, soil wetness is only meaningful over ice-free land; if a user selects it over the ocean, EarthScope explains why and suggests other variables instead of silently giving a wrong answer).

- Where is it changing? Users can search any place name, click anywhere on a world map, type coordinates, draw a rectangle (2°–9° per side), select a country boundary, or draw/upload a custom polygon (GeoJSON). Regions are analysed as exact area-weighted averages of every NASA grid cell inside them.

- How much is it changing? EarthScope computes the ordinary least-squares (OLS) slope and the robust Sen’s slope, in the variable’s own units per year and per decade, each with a 95% confidence interval.

- IS the change significant? It applies the regression t-test and the Mann-Kendall trend test at α = 0.05 and gives a clear verdict: significant increase, significant decrease, not significant, or mixed evidence (when tests disagree, it explains why).

How it works

1. The user follows a guided three-step flow: choose a variable, choose a place, choose a time period (minimum 10 years, 1981 to present).

2. The FastAPI backend requests real monthly data from the NASA POWER API for exactly the selected coordinates or region. Nothing is simulated or hard-coded.

3. Data are cleaned: NASA fill values (-999) are treated as missing, never zero-filled or interpolated.

4. Annual values are computed as day-weighted means; years with fewer than 10 valid months are excluded from the tests and shown as gaps.

5. Trend statistics are calculated. Because Earth science time series are often autocorrelated (one year influences the next), EarthScope also runs diagnostics (lag-1 autocorrelation, ACF, Ljung–Box) and autocorrelation-aware methods (Hamed–Rao modified Mann-Kendall, Newey–West standard errors), so users are not misled by over-confident p-values.

6. Results are shown as interactive charts (monthly and annual series with trend line), result cards, a statistics panel, a data table and a rule-based plain-language interpretation, with CSV/JSON/GeoJSON downloads and the exact NASA request URL for full transparency.

Key features that address the challenge

- Spatial Trend Explorer: the challenge notes that a variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another. EarthScope calculates the trend of every grid cell in a region and maps its magnitude, direction and significance, so opposing local trends are visible instead of hidden in an average. It corrects for testing many cells at once using Benjamini–Hochberg / Benjamini–Yekutieli false-discovery-rate control.

- Compare mode: up to three locations side by side with identical methods, including a "change versus own average" view.

- Country and polygon analysis: whole countries (e.g., Sri Lanka) or custom areas, with each cell weighted by its exact area inside the boundary; very large areas run as background jobs with progress tracking.

- Learning support for the target audience (high school and college students and the public): a Learn section explains time series, trends, regression, Mann-Kendall, p-values, confidence intervals and the difference between a trend and its cause. Example locations on six continents and built-in examples let users see how the tool works immediately.

- "Ask me" AI assistant: an optional chat on each results page that summarizes the findings in simple language and answers follow-up questions about them.

- Honest science: EarthScope states its limitations (grid-cell resolution, model-based data, limited power of short records) and reminds users that "not significant" does not mean "no change": sometimes a longer record is all a trend needs to become significant.

Benefits

- Makes NASA Earth data usable by anyone with a browser: no coding, downloads, accounts or API keys.

- Protects against false conclusions by testing significance and accounting for autocorrelation and multiple testing.

- Supports education, local awareness and decisions related to agriculture, water and heat, with a focus on our home country, Sri Lanka, while working anywhere on Earth.

What we hope to achieve

We want every student, teacher and community to be able to ask "Is my area getting hotter, drier or more humid?" and get an answer that is both understandable and scientifically sound. Next, we plan to add more NASA variables (precipitation from GPM/MERRA-2, vegetation health from MODIS NDVI, evaporation and streamflow from GLDAS), district-level boundaries, seasonal trend analysis and Sinhala/Tamil language support.

Tools and technologies

- Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts (charts), Leaflet / React Leaflet (maps), React Router.

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall (Mann-Kendall), Shapely and pyproj (geospatial area weighting).

- Background jobs: PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy/Alembic, Redis, RQ, Docker Compose.

- AI assistant: Google Gemini API (server-side only).

- Hosting: Vercel (frontend) and Render (backend).

- Quality: 497 automated backend tests and 74 frontend tests; statistical results independently validated against statsmodels, pymannkendall, SciPy and from-scratch reference implementations, plus live scripts that recompute results from raw NASA data
